subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Heckscher-Ohlin Theory and Factor Price Equalization

subjective.question: What is the concept of opportunity cost? How does it determine the specialization strategy of nations under the comparative advantage principle of international trade?
subjective.answer: Opportunity cost is the amount of one good that must be sacrificed (given up) in order to produce one additional unit of another good. Because resources are limited, producing more of one good necessarily means producing less of another, and the output forgone is the real cost of production. In international trade, each nation compares the opportunity costs of the two goods at home with those abroad. A nation has a comparative advantage in the good whose opportunity cost is lower than in the other nation. According to the principle of comparative advantage, each nation therefore specializes in producing and exporting the good in which its opportunity cost is lowest, and imports the good in which its opportunity cost is highest. In this way, opportunity cost directly determines the specialization strategy of nations: resources in each country move into the industry where the sacrifice per unit of output is smallest, world output rises, and both nations gain from exchange.

subjective.question: Distinguish between absolute advantage and comparative advantage.
subjective.answer: Absolute advantage, explained by Adam Smith, means that a nation can produce a good with fewer resources (for example, fewer labour hours) than another nation; it is an absolute comparison of efficiency in a single good. Comparative advantage, explained by David Ricardo, is a relative concept: a nation has a comparative advantage in the good that it produces at a lower opportunity cost than its partner, even if it has an absolute disadvantage in both goods. Absolute advantage compares one nation's efficiency in a good against the other nation's efficiency in the same good, while comparative advantage compares the ratio of efficiencies across two goods. Trade based on comparative advantage benefits both nations, whereas absolute advantage alone cannot explain why a nation that is less efficient in everything can still gain from trade.

subjective.question: State and explain the law of comparative advantage.
subjective.answer: The law of comparative advantage, given by David Ricardo, states that even if one nation is less efficient than (has an absolute disadvantage with respect to) the other nation in the production of both commodities, there is still a basis for mutually beneficial trade. The less efficient nation should specialize in and export the commodity in which its absolute disadvantage is smallest (this is its comparative advantage) and import the commodity in which its absolute disadvantage is greatest (its comparative disadvantage). Symmetrically, the more efficient nation should specialize in and export the commodity in which its absolute advantage is greatest. Specialization raises total world output, and exchange at a price ratio between the two domestic ratios allows both nations to consume more than they could in autarky.

subjective.question: What are the main assumptions of the Ricardian theory of comparative advantage?
subjective.answer: (i) There are only two nations and two commodities. (ii) Labour is the only factor of production, and the cost of a good is measured by its labour content. (iii) Labour is perfectly mobile within a nation but completely immobile between nations. (iv) Labour productivity (technology) differs between nations but is constant within each nation, so opportunity costs are constant and the production possibility frontier is a straight line. (v) There is perfect competition in the goods and labour markets. (vi) There are no transport costs and no barriers to trade. (vii) There is full employment of labour. (viii) Technology is given and fixed. Under these assumptions, differences in labour productivity are the source of comparative advantage, and specialization in trade is complete.

subjective.question: Why is specialization complete under constant opportunity costs but incomplete under increasing opportunity costs?
subjective.answer: Under constant opportunity costs, the domestic price ratio does not change as production expands. When the world price ratio differs from the domestic ratio, it therefore remains profitable to keep shifting resources into the comparative-advantage good until the nation produces only that good, so specialization is complete. Under increasing opportunity costs, however, expanding production of the export good steadily raises its opportunity cost. Specialization proceeds only until the rising domestic opportunity cost becomes equal to the world price ratio; beyond that point, producing still more of the export good would cost more than it can earn in trade. The nation therefore continues to produce some of the import-competing good as well, and specialization is incomplete.

subjective.question: Explain why a nation can gain from trade even if it is less efficient than its partner in the production of both goods.
subjective.answer: Absolute efficiency in both goods does not remove the difference in relative efficiency. The less efficient nation is relatively less disadvantaged in one of the two goods — the good in which its opportunity cost is lower — and that good is its comparative advantage. By specializing in it and exchanging at an international price ratio lying between the two domestic price ratios, the nation obtains the other good more cheaply, in terms of output forgone, than by producing it at home. Its consumption possibilities therefore expand beyond its own production possibility frontier, and it gains from trade even though its partner is absolutely more efficient in the production of both goods.

subjective.question: Why may a large nation fail to specialize completely in its comparative-advantage good?
subjective.answer: A small nation can sell its export good at the prevailing world price without affecting that price, so it can specialize completely. A large nation, however, supplies a substantial share of the world market. As it expands production and exports of its comparative-advantage good, the world supply of that good rises and its world price falls, so the terms of trade move against the large nation. Beyond a certain point the extra output earns so little that further specialization no longer pays, and the nation keeps producing the import-competing good as well. The same reasoning applies on the demand side: the large nation's demand for imports is big enough to raise import prices. Large nations therefore typically show incomplete specialization.

subjective.question: Explain the meaning of incomplete specialization with reference to increasing opportunity costs.
subjective.answer: Incomplete specialization means that even after trade opens, a nation continues to produce both goods — its export good and the import-competing good — instead of producing only the export good. It arises under increasing opportunity costs: as resources are shifted into the export industry, the opportunity cost of the export good rises steadily. Specialization stops being worthwhile when the domestic opportunity cost ratio becomes equal to the world price ratio; from that point, producing the import good at home is no more costly than importing it, so domestic production of both goods continues. Incomplete specialization is also the normal situation for large nations, whose own trade moves world prices against them.

subjective.question: What are the gains from trade? Distinguish between production gains and consumption gains.
subjective.answer: The gains from trade are the increase in output and consumption that a nation obtains by specializing according to comparative advantage and exchanging with other nations, compared with the no-trade (autarky) position. They are of two kinds. (i) Production gains: specialization reallocates world resources to their relatively most efficient uses, so total world output increases with the same resources, each nation producing the good in which it is relatively most efficient. (ii) Consumption (exchange) gains: because the nation trades at world prices that differ from its domestic price ratio, it can consume a bundle of goods lying outside its own production possibility frontier. Together, the two gains allow both trading nations to reach a higher level of consumption and welfare than in autarky.

subjective.question: China and Singapore can produce soybeans and palm oil with the following labour requirements (hours per unit): China - soybeans 8, palm oil 4; Singapore - soybeans 1, palm oil 2. Assume that China trades 8 units of soybeans against 8 units of palm oil (8 units of soybeans = 8 units of palm oil) with Singapore. Calculate the gains from trade in terms of production for both China and Singapore using the law of comparative advantage.
subjective.answer: The table gives the labour hours required to produce one unit of each good: China needs 8 hours for soybeans and 4 hours for palm oil; Singapore needs 1 hour for soybeans and 2 hours for palm oil. Step 1 - Opportunity costs. In China, one unit of soybeans costs 8/4 = 2 units of palm oil, and one unit of palm oil costs 4/8 = 0.5 unit of soybeans. In Singapore, one unit of soybeans costs 1/2 = 0.5 unit of palm oil, and one unit of palm oil costs 2/1 = 2 units of soybeans. Step 2 - Comparative advantage. Singapore has the lower opportunity cost in soybeans (0.5 < 2 units of palm oil), so Singapore specializes in soybeans. China has the lower opportunity cost in palm oil (0.5 < 2 units of soybeans), so China specializes in palm oil. Note that Singapore has an absolute advantage in both goods, since it needs fewer hours for each, yet trade is still mutually beneficial. Step 3 - Gains at the exchange ratio 8 units of soybeans = 8 units of palm oil (that is, 1 soybean = 1 palm oil, which lies between the domestic ratios of 0.5 and 2). China exports 8 units of palm oil, which cost it 8 x 4 = 32 labour hours, and receives 8 units of soybeans. Producing 8 units of soybeans at home would have cost China 8 x 8 = 64 labour hours, so China saves 64 - 32 = 32 labour hours; equivalently, with 64 hours China can obtain 16 units of soybeans through trade instead of only 8 at home. Singapore exports 8 units of soybeans, which cost it 8 x 1 = 8 labour hours, and receives 8 units of palm oil. Producing 8 units of palm oil at home would have cost Singapore 8 x 2 = 16 labour hours, so Singapore saves 16 - 8 = 8 labour hours; equivalently, with 16 hours Singapore can obtain 16 units of palm oil through trade instead of only 8 at home. Hence both nations gain from trade in terms of production: the same traded quantities are obtained with 40 fewer labour hours in total, and the labour released can be used to produce additional output.

subjective.question: On what factors does the size of the gains from trade depend?
subjective.answer: (i) The difference between the domestic price (opportunity cost) ratios of the two nations: the greater the difference, the larger the potential gains from trade. (ii) The terms of trade: the closer the international price ratio settles to a nation's own domestic ratio, the smaller that nation's share of the gains; the farther away, the larger its share. (iii) The relative size of the nations: a small nation trading with a large one generally obtains the larger share of the gains, because trade takes place near the large nation's domestic price ratio. (iv) The strength and elasticity of reciprocal demand, which determine where the terms of trade settle. (v) Transport costs and trade barriers, which reduce the net gains.

subjective.question: "Trade is a positive-sum game." Explain this statement.
subjective.answer: A zero-sum game is one in which one side's gain is exactly equal to the other side's loss. International trade is not like that. Because nations specialize according to comparative advantage, total world output rises while world resources are unchanged, so the total to be shared becomes bigger. Both nations can simultaneously consume more of the traded goods than they could without trade: each moves to a consumption point outside its own production possibility frontier. The division of the gains between the two nations depends on the terms of trade, but the sum of the gains is positive. This is why trade differs fundamentally from the mercantilist view that a nation can gain only at another nation's expense.

subjective.question: Explain, with a small numerical example, how specialization according to comparative advantage increases world output.
subjective.answer: Suppose each nation has 200 labour hours. Nation A produces one unit of cloth with 10 hours and one unit of wine with 20 hours; Nation B produces one unit of cloth with 20 hours and one unit of wine with 10 hours. In autarky, each nation divides its labour equally between the two goods. Nation A produces 100/10 = 10 units of cloth and 100/20 = 5 units of wine. Nation B produces 100/20 = 5 units of cloth and 100/10 = 10 units of wine. World output without trade is therefore 15 units of cloth and 15 units of wine. Opportunity costs show that A has a comparative advantage in cloth (1 cloth costs 0.5 wine, against 2 wine in B) and B has a comparative advantage in wine (1 wine costs 0.5 cloth, against 2 cloth in A). With complete specialization, A uses all 200 hours for cloth and produces 20 units, while B uses all 200 hours for wine and produces 20 units. World output rises to 20 units of cloth and 20 units of wine - an increase of 5 units of each good from the same world resources. If the two nations now exchange at 1 cloth = 1 wine and each exports 7 units of its specialized good, A consumes 13 cloth and 7 wine (instead of 10 and 5) and B consumes 7 cloth and 13 wine (instead of 5 and 10), so both nations gain.

subjective.topic: Heckscher-Ohlin Theory and Factor Price Equalization
subjective.question: Explain the factor price equalization theorem of international trade.
subjective.answer: The factor price equalization theorem, derived from the Heckscher-Ohlin theory and formally proved by Paul Samuelson, states that free international trade in goods will equalize the relative and absolute prices of homogeneous factors of production - such as the wage rate for similar labour and the return on capital - between trading nations. The mechanism is as follows. A labour-abundant nation exports labour-intensive goods; expanding that industry raises the demand for labour and pushes its wage up, while the return on its scarce capital falls. In the capital-abundant partner, exports of capital-intensive goods raise the return to capital, while imports of labour-intensive goods reduce the demand for labour and push its wage down. Trade in goods thus acts as a substitute for the international movement of factors themselves: exporting a labour-intensive good is indirectly exporting labour services. Under the theorem's assumptions - identical technology, perfect competition, no transport costs or trade barriers, and both nations continuing to produce both goods - trade equalizes commodity prices, and with the same commodity prices and identical technology, profit maximization leads firms in both nations to pay identical factor prices. In practice the equalization is only partial, because of transport costs, tariffs, differences in technology and imperfect competition.

subjective.topic: Heckscher-Ohlin Theory and Factor Price Equalization
subjective.question: State the Heckscher-Ohlin theorem. On what basis does it explain comparative advantage?
subjective.answer: The Heckscher-Ohlin theorem states that a nation will export the commodity whose production requires the intensive use of the nation's relatively abundant (and therefore cheap) factor of production, and will import the commodity whose production requires the intensive use of the nation's relatively scarce (and therefore expensive) factor. The theory explains comparative advantage by differences in factor endowments between nations. Because one nation is relatively rich in labour and another relatively rich in capital, relative factor prices differ in autarky: the labour-abundant nation can produce labour-intensive goods relatively cheaply, and the capital-abundant nation can produce capital-intensive goods relatively cheaply. Unlike Ricardo, who attributed trade to unexplained differences in labour productivity, Heckscher and Ohlin trace the cause of trade to this underlying difference in the relative supply of factors.

subjective.topic: Heckscher-Ohlin Theory and Factor Price Equalization
subjective.question: Define factor abundance and factor intensity.
subjective.answer: Factor abundance describes a nation's overall endowment of one factor relative to another, compared with its trading partner. It can be defined in two ways. (i) Physical definition: a nation is capital-abundant if its total stock of capital relative to its total labour force (K/L) is greater than that of the other nation. (ii) Price definition: a nation is capital-abundant if the price of capital relative to the price of labour (r/w) is lower in it than in the other nation. Factor intensity describes the production of a single good: a good is labour-intensive if, at given factor prices, it is produced with a higher ratio of labour to capital than the other good, and capital-intensive if it is produced with a higher ratio of capital to labour than the other good.

subjective.topic: Heckscher-Ohlin Theory and Factor Price Equalization
subjective.question: What conditions must hold for factor prices to be completely equalized through trade?
subjective.answer: (i) The two nations have identical technology, that is, the same production functions. (ii) There is perfect competition in goods and factor markets. (iii) Trade is completely free, with no transport costs, tariffs or other barriers, so that commodity prices are fully equalized between the nations. (iv) Both nations continue to produce both goods after trade opens (incomplete specialization), so each factor remains employed in both industries in each nation. (v) Factors of production are homogeneous and of the same quality in both nations. (vi) There is no factor-intensity reversal, and factor prices are flexible. If any of these conditions fails, as they generally do in reality, factor price equalization through trade is incomplete.

subjective.topic: Heckscher-Ohlin Theory and Factor Price Equalization
subjective.question: What is the Leontief paradox? What does it imply for the Heckscher-Ohlin theory?
subjective.answer: In 1953, Wassily Leontief tested the Heckscher-Ohlin theorem with United States data. Since the United States was the most capital-abundant nation in the world, the theorem predicted that it would export capital-intensive goods and import labour-intensive goods. Leontief found the opposite: United States exports were more labour-intensive than its imports. This contradiction of the theorem became known as the Leontief paradox. It implies that factor endowments alone cannot fully explain the pattern of trade; other influences, such as differences in labour skills and productivity, human capital, technology, natural resources and demand conditions, must also be taken into account. The paradox stimulated extensive further research and more refined versions of trade theory, although the Heckscher-Ohlin framework remains a central explanation of trade based on resource endowments.

subjective.topic: Heckscher-Ohlin Theory and Factor Price Equalization
subjective.question: Explain how free trade in goods leads to the equalization of factor prices between nations.
subjective.answer: Consider two nations, one abundant in labour (so wages are low and the return to capital is high) and the other abundant in capital (so wages are high and the return to capital is low). Before trade, these factor price differences make labour-intensive goods cheap in the first nation and capital-intensive goods cheap in the second. When trade opens, each nation exports the good that uses its abundant factor intensively. In the labour-abundant nation, expanding production of the labour-intensive export good raises the demand for labour, so wages rise, while the contracting capital-intensive industry releases capital and its return falls. In the capital-abundant nation the opposite happens: demand for capital rises and its return increases, while demand for labour falls and wages decline. Trade therefore raises the price of each nation's abundant factor and lowers the price of its scarce factor, driving factor prices in the two nations toward each other. The process continues until, under the ideal assumptions of the theory (identical technology, no transport costs, incomplete specialization), commodity prices, and with them factor prices, are fully equalized - trade has achieved the same result as if the factors themselves had moved between the nations.

subjective.topic: Heckscher-Ohlin Theory and Factor Price Equalization
subjective.question: Compare the Ricardian and Heckscher-Ohlin explanations of the basis of international trade.
subjective.answer: Both theories agree that international trade is based on comparative advantage and that it benefits both trading nations. They differ in explaining why comparative advantage exists. Ricardo attributes it to differences in labour productivity (technology) between nations and takes those differences as given, without explaining them; labour is the only factor of production in his model. Heckscher and Ohlin explain comparative advantage by differences in factor endowments: a nation has a cost advantage in the goods that use its abundant factor intensively, because the abundant factor is relatively cheap. The Heckscher-Ohlin model therefore works with two factors of production (labour and capital), assumes identical technology in the two nations, and gives a deeper explanation of trade which also leads to further results such as the factor price equalization theorem.

subjective.topic: Heckscher-Ohlin Theory and Factor Price Equalization
subjective.question: Discuss the main limitations of the factor price equalization theorem in the real world.
subjective.answer: (i) Technology is not identical across nations; differences in productivity keep wage differences alive even with free trade. (ii) Transport costs and tariffs prevent the complete equalization of commodity prices, so factor prices cannot fully converge. (iii) Factors are not homogeneous: labour differs in skill, education and quality between nations. (iv) Markets are imperfectly competitive and some factor prices are rigid, for example because of minimum wage laws. (v) Many nations specialize completely in some products, violating the incomplete-specialization condition of the theorem. (vi) Some factors, such as land and natural resources, are specific to particular locations and cannot be matched across countries. For these reasons, the theorem describes a tendency - trade narrows international factor price differences - rather than the complete equalization that is actually observed.

subjective.question: Define the terms of trade. How are the net barter terms of trade measured?
subjective.answer: The terms of trade of a nation are the ratio of the prices of its exports to the prices of its imports; they show how much of imports a nation can obtain in exchange for a given quantity of its exports. The most commonly used measure is the net barter (commodity) terms of trade, N = (Px / Pm) x 100, where Px is the index of export prices and Pm is the index of import prices. In the base year the index is equal to 100. If the index rises above 100, the terms of trade have improved: export prices have risen relative to import prices, so each unit of exports buys more imports. If the index falls below 100, the terms of trade have deteriorated: export prices have fallen relative to import prices, and the nation must export more to obtain the same quantity of imports.

subjective.question: Suppose there are only two nations trading two commodities X and Y with each other. The initial value of the terms of trade of nation 1 and nation 2 is 100. (a) If the terms of trade of nation 1 rose from 100 to 130, what does it imply about export prices in nation 1 relative to its import prices? (b) If the terms of trade of nation 1 rose from 100 to 130, what does it imply about nation 2's terms of trade?
subjective.answer: (a) The terms of trade of nation 1, N = (Px / Pm) x 100, have risen from 100 to 130. This means that nation 1's export prices have risen by 30 percent relative to its import prices. Equivalently, nation 1 can now obtain 30 percent more imports in exchange for the same quantity of exports than before; its terms of trade have improved. (b) In a two-nation world, the two nations' terms of trade are exact reciprocals of each other, because nation 1's export prices are nation 2's import prices and nation 1's import prices are nation 2's export prices. Nation 2's terms of trade therefore fall to N2 = (1 / 1.30) x 100 = 76.9 approximately. Nation 2's terms of trade have deteriorated from 100 to about 76.9: its export prices have fallen relative to its import prices, and it must now export more to obtain the same quantity of imports. In the two-nation case, one nation's improvement is thus necessarily the other nation's deterioration.

subjective.question: Distinguish between the net barter, gross barter and income terms of trade.
subjective.answer: (i) Net barter (commodity) terms of trade compare prices: N = (Px / Pm) x 100, where Px and Pm are the export and import price indices. (ii) Gross barter terms of trade compare quantities: G = (Qm / Qx) x 100, the ratio of the total quantity of imports to the total quantity of exports; this measure is relevant where trade is conducted by barter, without money prices. (iii) Income terms of trade measure the nation's capacity to import: I = N x Qx = (Px / Pm) x Qx, that is, the commodity terms of trade multiplied by the index of the volume of exports. The income terms of trade can improve even when the commodity terms of trade deteriorate, provided the volume of exports rises sufficiently, because they show the total quantity of imports that the nation's export earnings can buy.

subjective.question: How are the equilibrium terms of trade between two nations determined?
subjective.answer: The equilibrium terms of trade are determined by reciprocal demand - the strength and elasticity of each nation's demand for the other nation's good - a concept developed by John Stuart Mill. Each nation's domestic opportunity cost ratio sets a limit to the possible range: trade can only benefit both nations at a ratio lying between the two domestic price ratios, because outside those limits one nation would gain nothing or would lose. Within those limits, the exact ratio is settled by reciprocal demand. If nation 1's demand for nation 2's good is very strong and inelastic, the terms of trade settle close to nation 1's domestic ratio and nation 1 obtains only a small share of the gains; if its demand is weak and elastic, the ratio settles near the partner's domestic ratio and nation 1 captures most of the gains. Equilibrium is reached at the ratio at which the value of each nation's desired exports exactly pays for its desired imports, so that trade is balanced.

subjective.question: What are the effects of an improvement in the terms of trade on a nation's welfare?
subjective.answer: An improvement in the terms of trade means that the nation receives higher prices for its exports relative to the prices it pays for its imports. With the same quantity of exports, it can now import a larger quantity of goods, so its consumption possibilities expand and its real income and welfare rise; resources that would have been needed to produce those additional imports at home are released for other uses. Conversely, a deterioration in the terms of trade reduces the imports obtainable from a given volume of exports and lowers real income. An improvement is not an unmixed blessing in every respect - it worsens the trading partner's position and can hurt domestic industries that compete with the now cheaper imports - but, other things equal, an improvement in the terms of trade raises the nation's overall welfare.
